chips: pra + √mā + ana (lyuṭ): “that by which one measures”
pra + √mā + ya (yat): “what is to be measured”, ā→e
pra + √yuj + ana (lyuṭ): “what one is engaged toward”
dṛṣṭa (√dṛś + ta: “seen”) + anta (“end”): a settled, seen instance
siddha (√sidh + ta: “accomplished”) + anta: the accomplished end
nis + √nī + a: “leading out to a conclusion” (n→ṇ)
chala “disguise, trickery” (traditionally from a root chal; not in the dhātupāṭha)
niḥśreyasa (nis + śreyas “better”: “beyond the good”) + adhigama (adhi + √gam + a)
1.1.1.tr: From true knowledge of these sixteen topics comes the attainment of the highest good.
1.1.1.ex: It lists the whole syllabus in one compound (the uddeśa, the naming) and states the payoff: the highest good comes from truly knowing these sixteen topics. The rest of the text defines and examines them.

chips: duḥ (“bad”) + kha (“space”): traditional etymology, “a bad axle-hole”
uttara-uttara (“each later”) + apāya (apa + √i + a: “going away”) + loc. -e
the one just before it goes too
tad + an-antara (“with no gap”) + apāya + abl. -āt
1.1.2.tr: Of pain, birth, activity, fault and false cognition: as each later one departs, the one before it departs, and so there is release.
1.1.2.ex: A chain of causes read backwards. False cognition produces faults (desire, aversion, delusion); faults drive activity; activity leads to birth; birth is where pain lives. Remove the root, and each result goes in turn, ending in apavarga.

chips: prati + akṣa (“sense organ, eye”): “before the sense”
are the means of valid knowledge
1.1.3.tr: Perception, inference, analogy and testimony are the means of valid knowledge.
1.1.3.ex: States the four sources of valid knowledge. The text goes on to define each of them (1.1.4 to 1.1.7), and adhyāya 2 defends them against objections.

1.1.4.iast: indriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānam avyapadeśyam avyabhicāri vyavasāyātmakaṃ pratyakṣam
chips: indra (“lord”: the self) + iya: “belonging to the lord (self)”
“aim, object, meaning” (traditionally from the root ṛ “to reach”; derivation uncertain)
sannikarṣa (sam + ni + √kṛṣ + a: “drawing close”) + utpanna (ut + √pad + na: “arisen”)
a + vi + apa + √diś + ya (ṇyat): “not to be pointed out (by a word)”
vyavasāya (vi + ava + √so + a: “settling, determination”) + ātmaka (ātman + ka): “having it as its nature”
1.1.4.tr: Perception is cognition born of contact between a sense and its object, not tied to a word, non-erring, and determinate.
1.1.4.ex: Four conditions define perception: it arises from contact of a sense with its object; it is not merely verbal; it does not err; and it is determinate. Each phrase excludes a wrong case, such as hallucination (which errs) or a bare word (which is not born of contact).
1.1.4.dev: इन्द्रियार्थसन्निकर्षोत्पन्नं ज्ञानम् अव्यपदेश्यम् अव्यभिचारि व्यवसायात्मकं प्रत्यक्षम्
1.1.4.corpus: indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam jñānam avyapadeśyam avyabhicāri vyavasāyātmakam pratyakṣam

1.1.5.iast: atha tatpūrvakaṃ trividham anumānaṃ pūrvavat śeṣavat sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ ca
chips: tad + pūrva + ka: “having that as antecedent”
śeṣa (√śiṣ + a: “what is left over”) + vat
1.1.5.tr: Then inference, which is preceded by perception, is of three kinds: pūrvavat, śeṣavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa.
1.1.5.ex: Inference comes after perception: you perceive a sign, then infer what it points to. Three types are named; commentators illustrate them with clouds to rain (cause to effect), a flooded river to rain upstream (effect to cause), and the sun’s motion (general likeness). Readings differ.
1.1.5.dev: अथ तत्पूर्वकं त्रिविधम् अनुमानं पूर्ववत् शेषवत् सामान्यतोदृष्टं च
1.1.5.corpus: atha tatpūrvakaṃ trividham anumānaṃ pūrvavat śeṣavat sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ ca

chips: sa (“same”) + dharma + ya (ṣyañ): “sameness of property” + abl. -āt
1.1.6.tr: Analogy establishes what is to be known through similarity to something well known.
1.1.6.ex: You know something well; you are told a new thing resembles it; later you recognise the new thing from that likeness. The classic case is the cow and the gavaya.

1.1.7.tr: The instruction of a reliable person is verbal testimony.
1.1.7.ex: Testimony counts as knowledge only when it comes from a reliable person (āpta), who knows the matter and speaks it truly.

1.1.9.tr: The objects of valid knowledge are: self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, fault, rebirth, fruit, pain and release.
1.1.9.ex: The twelve things worth knowing, in the order the text defines them next (1.1.10 to 1.1.22). The list begins with the self and ends with release.

1.1.10.tr: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition are the marks of the self.
1.1.10.ex: The self cannot be seen, so it is inferred from marks that need a conscious subject: wanting, disliking, trying, feeling pleasure and pain, and knowing.

1.1.16.tr: That cognitions do not arise at the same moment is the mark of the mind.
1.1.16.ex: We cannot attend to two things at one instant. Nyāya concludes there is an internal organ, the mind, that lets in one cognition at a time.

1.1.23.iast: samānānekadharmopapatteḥ vipratipatteḥ upalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthātaḥ ca viśeṣāpekṣaḥ vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ
chips: from a common property, or from several (uncommon) properties
samāna “same, common”; aneka (an + eka: “not one”); dharma (√dhṛ + ma: “what upholds”, property); upapatti (upa + √pad + ti: “occurrence”)
from irregularity of perception and non-perception
upalabdhi (upa + √labh + ti: “perceiving”); an-upalabdhi; a-vyavasthā (vi + ava + √sthā + a: “settled order”) + tas (“from”)
1.1.23.tr: Doubt is a wavering that looks for a distinguishing feature, arising from a common property, an uncommon property, conflicting opinions, or irregularity in perceiving or not perceiving.
1.1.23.ex: Doubt is not just ignorance. It is a back-and-forth between alternatives, kept alive because something is shared between them (a tall shape that could be a post or a person) and nothing yet separates them.
1.1.23.dev: समानानेकधर्मोपपत्तेः विप्रतिपत्तेः उपलब्ध्यनुपलब्ध्यव्यवस्थातः च विशेषापेक्षः विमर्शः संशयः
1.1.23.corpus: samānānekadharmopapatteḥ vipratipatteḥ upalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthātaḥ ca viśeṣāpekṣaḥ vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ

1.1.32.tr: Thesis, reason, example, application and conclusion are the members of an argument.
1.1.32.ex: The members of a full, communicable argument. Nyāya wants all five; other schools accept fewer.

1.1.33.tr: Stating what is to be established is the thesis.
1.1.33.ex: The thesis names the subject and what is claimed of it: “the hill has fire.”

1.1.34.tr: The reason establishes what is to be established through similarity to the example.
1.1.34.ex: The reason links the subject to the target through what the example shows: “because of smoke”, as in the kitchen.

chips: vi + dharma + ya (ṣyañ): “difference of property” + abl. -āt
1.1.35.ex: The same reason can be shown from the other side: where the target is absent the reason is absent too, as in a lake.

1.1.36.tr: An instance that shares the property of the sādhya, through similarity to it, is the example.
1.1.36.ex: The example is a familiar instance where the target and reason both occur, so everyone agrees: the kitchen has fire and smoke.

1.1.37.tr: Or, from the reverse, the opposite kind of example.
1.1.37.ex: The opposite kind of example is a case lacking the property of the target (and the reason), such as a lake.

1.1.38.iast: udāharaṇāpekṣaḥ tathā iti upasaṃhāraḥ na tathā iti vā sādhyasya upanayaḥ
1.1.38.tr: Depending on the example, saying “so it is” or “not so” about the subject is the application.
1.1.38.ex: The application ties the subject back to the example: “and this hill is likewise smoky”, or in the negative form, “not so”.
1.1.38.dev: उदाहरणापेक्षः तथा इति उपसंहारः न तथा इति वा साध्यस्य उपनयः
1.1.38.corpus: udāharaṇāpekṣaḥ tathā iti upasaṃhāraḥ na tathā iti vā sādhyasya upanayaḥ

1.1.39.tr: Restating the thesis after the reason has been cited is the conclusion.
1.1.39.ex: The conclusion restates the thesis, now supported by reason and example.

1.1.40.iast: avijñātatattve arthe kāraṇopapattitaḥ tattvajñānārtham ūhaḥ tarkaḥ
chips: about a thing whose truth is not known
a + vi + √jñā + ta (“not known”) + tattva (tad + tva) + artha + loc. -e
on the strength of causal considerations
for the sake of knowing the truth
1.1.40.tr: Tarka is a supposition, made on causal grounds about a thing whose truth is not yet known, in order to reach knowledge of the truth.
1.1.40.ex: Tarka is not itself proof. It is a probing supposition that tests an alternative (“suppose it were so; then absurdity follows”), and so helps reach the truth.
1.1.40.dev: अविज्ञाततत्त्वे अर्थे कारणोपपत्तितः तत्त्वज्ञानार्थम् ऊहः तर्कः
1.1.40.corpus: avijñātatatve arthe kāraṇopapattitaḥ tattvajñānārtham uhaḥ tarkaḥ

1.1.41.tr: Having weighed it with thesis and counter-thesis, settling the matter is ascertainment.
1.1.41.ex: Ascertainment comes after weighing both sides, not from assertion alone.

chips: proving and refuting by pramāṇa and tarka
pramāṇa; tarka; sādhana (√sādh + ana); upālambha (upa + ā + √labh + a: “censure, refutation”)
taking up a thesis and its counter-thesis
1.2.1.tr: Vāda: proving and refuting by pramāṇa and tarka, within the accepted tenet, with the five members, taking a thesis and counter-thesis.
1.2.1.ex: Vāda is the honest debate: both sides can state and prove a thesis, the five members are used, and the accepted doctrine is not contradicted.

chips: quibble, futile rejoinder, ground of defeat
chala; jāti (√jan + ti); nigrahasthāna (ni + √grah + a; √sthā + ana)
1.2.2.tr: Jalpa has those same features but proves and refutes also by chala, jāti and nigrahasthāna.
1.2.2.ex: Jalpa allows the debater to win by any permitted means: chala, jāti and nigrahasthāna become tools.

chips: lacking the establishing of a counter-thesis
pratipakṣa; sthāpanā (√sthā + ṇic + yuc + ā: “establishing”); hīna (√hā + na: “deprived of”)
1.2.3.tr: That same, without establishing a counter-thesis of one’s own, is vitaṇḍā.
1.2.3.ex: Vitaṇḍā is jalpa stripped of any thesis of one’s own: it only criticises.

1.2.4.tr: The deviating, contradictory, question-balancing, sādhya-equal and out-of-time reasons are the hetvābhāsas.
1.2.4.ex: Five ways a reason can fail while looking like a reason: it deviates, contradicts, leaves the question as it was, is as unproven as the target, or comes out of time. Note the “-sama” naming: “equal to” the question, “equal to” the sādhya.

1.2.5.tr: The inconclusive reason is the deviating one (savyabhicāra).
1.2.5.ex: A reason present both where the target is and where it is not proves nothing. “Knowable, therefore eternal” is the stock case, since knowable includes non-eternal things.

1.2.6.tr: A reason that contradicts the very tenet one has accepted is viruddha.
1.2.6.ex: A reason that contradicts the doctrine the speaker himself accepts, and so proves the opposite of what he wants.

1.2.7.iast: yasmāt prakaraṇacintā saḥ nirṇayārtham apadiṣṭaḥ prakaraṇasamaḥ
chips: the question itself stays under consideration
1.2.7.tr: A reason cited to settle a question, from which the question itself remains live, is prakaraṇasama.
1.2.7.ex: A reason that leaves the question exactly where it was: the same sort of reason can be given for the opposite.
1.2.7.dev: यस्मात् प्रकरणचिन्ता सः निर्णयार्थम् अपदिष्टः प्रकरणसमः

1.2.8.tr: A reason no different from the sādhya, since it too needs to be established, is sādhyasama.
1.2.8.ex: A reason that needs proving just as much as the thesis, so it settles nothing.

chips: cited after the time has passed
kāla; atyaya (ati + √i + a: “passing by”); apadiṣṭa (apa + √diś + ta)
1.2.9.tr: A reason cited after its time has lapsed is kālātīta.
1.2.9.ex: A reason presented after its moment has passed. Tradition links this with the later bādhita, a reason whose conclusion is already contradicted by a stronger means of knowledge.

chips: artha; vikalpa (vi + √kḷp + a: “alternative”); upapatti (upa + √pad + ti) + instr. -yā
1.2.10.tr: Obstructing a statement by supposing a different meaning for it is chala.
1.2.10.ex: Chala is not an error of fact. It twists the meaning of a statement in order to refute something the speaker did not say.

1.2.11.iast: tat trividham vākchalaṃ sāmānyacchalam upacāracchalaṃ ca iti
1.2.11.tr: It is threefold: quibble on wording, on generality, and on figurative use.
1.2.11.ex: Three ways of twisting: through the wording (vāk), by over-generalising (sāmānya), or by taking figurative use (upacāra) literally.
1.2.11.dev: तत् त्रिविधम् वाक्छलं सामान्यच्छलम् उपचारच्छलं च इति
1.2.11.corpus: tat trividham - vākchalam sāmānyacchalam upacāracchalam ca iti

1.2.12.iast: aviśeṣābhihite arthe vaktuḥ abhiprāyāt arthāntarakalpanā vākchalam
chips: when a word with several senses is used
a + viśeṣa; abhihita (abhi + √dhā + ta: “said”); artha + loc. -e
vaktṛ (√vac + tṛ: “speaker”) gen.; abhi + pra + √i + a: “intention” + abl.
artha; antara “other”; kalpanā (√kḷp + ṇic + yuc + ā: “imagining”)
1.2.12.tr: When a word with more than one sense is used, imagining a meaning other than the speaker intended is vākchala.
1.2.12.ex: The standard illustration is “navakambalo ’yaṃ māṇavakaḥ”: nava means both “new” and “nine”, so the quibbler objects “he has only one blanket, not nine.”
1.2.12.dev: अविशेषाभिहिते अर्थे वक्तुः अभिप्रायात् अर्थान्तरकल्पना वाक्छलम्
1.2.12.corpus: aviśeṣābhihite arthe vaktuḥ abhiprāyāt arthāntarakalpanā vākchalam

chips: of a thing that is possible
by stretching the generality too far
a + sam + √bhū + ta; artha; kalpanā (√kḷp + ṇic + yuc)
1.2.13.tr: Taking a possible statement and stretching its generality to read an impossible meaning into it is sāmānyacchala.
1.2.13.ex: The speaker says something reasonable about a class; the quibbler stretches it to cover a member it was never meant to include.

chips: when a word is used in a transferred sense
dharma; vikalpa (vi + √kḷp + a); nirdeśa (nis + √diś + a) + loc. -e
denying it by taking it literally
artha; sat-bhāva (sat + √bhū + a: “existence”); prati-ṣedha (prati + √sidh² + a: “warding off, denial”)
1.2.14.tr: When a word is used figuratively, denying the statement by insisting on the literal sense is upacāracchala.
1.2.14.ex: The speaker uses a word figuratively (“the platforms shout” for “the people on them”); the quibbler insists on the literal sense and denies it.

chips: sa + dharma + ya; vi + dharma + ya; instr. dual -ābhyām
1.2.18.tr: A counter-position taken merely on similarity or dissimilarity is jāti, a futile rejoinder.
1.2.18.ex: A jāti looks like a refutation but rests on a bare likeness or unlikeness, without the pervasion (vyāpti) that real refutation would need.

1.2.19.tr: Misunderstanding and non-understanding are grounds of defeat.
1.2.19.ex: A debater loses if he misunderstands the matter or fails to understand it at all. This is the general statement; 5.2.1 lists 22 types.

chips: pratyakṣa (prati + akṣa); ādi “beginning, and so on”; gen. pl. -ām
are not valid means (the objector says)
because the three times cannot be made to work
traikālya (tri + kāla + ya: “the three times”) + a + √sidh + ti (ktin): “non-establishment”
2.1.8.tr: Objector: perception and the rest are not valid means, because they fail in all three times: before, after or together with their objects.
2.1.8.ex: The objector’s claim: a means of knowledge would have to stand in some time-relation to its object (before, after or together), and none of these works. Nyāya states the objection in its own text before answering it.

chips: the rejection itself cannot be established
2.1.13.tr: Reply: by rejecting every pramāṇa, the objector’s own rejection is left with nothing to establish it.
2.1.13.ex: The reply: to reject every pramāṇa, the objector must himself rely on one; so the rejection undoes itself.

chips: like the establishing of a lamp’s light
pradīpa (pra + √dīp + a: “lamp”); prakāśa (pra + √kāś + a: “light”); siddhi (√sidh + ti); vat “like”
since that is established (in the same way)
2.1.19.tr: No: it is established just as a lamp’s light is, which both shows other things and is itself known.
2.1.19.ex: Another reply: a means of knowledge is itself known and also shows other things, as a lamp’s light is seen and also shows a pot.

chips: darśana (√dṛś + ana: “seeing”); sparśana (√spṛś + ana: “touching”); instr. dual -ābhyām
since one and the same object is grasped
3.1.1.tr: Since one and the same object is grasped by seeing and by touching (there is a single knower, the self, apart from the separate senses).
3.1.1.ex: Seeing and touching are different senses with different domains. Yet one person says “I touch what I saw.” So there must be a single subject, apart from the senses, who grasps both.

chips: because each sense has its own fixed domain
viṣaya “sphere, domain (of a sense)”; vyavasthāna (vi + ava + √sthā + ana: “fixing”) + abl.
3.1.2.tr: Objector: not so, because each sense has its own fixed domain.
3.1.2.ex: The objection: each sense has its own fixed domain, so why posit a further knower?

chips: from that very fixing of domains
tad + vyavasthāna (vi + ava + √sthā + ana) + abl.; eva “just”
3.1.3.tr: Reply: that very fixing of domains shows there is a self that brings them together, so the argument stands.
3.1.3.ex: The reply: the fixing of domains is exactly why a single knower is needed, to bring the separate domains together.

chips: for guarding the ascertainment of truth
tattva (tad + tva); adhyavasāya (adhi + ava + √so + a: “resolve”); saṃrakṣaṇa (sam + √rakṣ + ana: “guarding”); artha “purpose”
for protecting the sprouting of seeds
like a fence of thorny branches
kaṇṭaka “thorn”; śākhā “branch”; āvaraṇa (ā + √vṛ + ana: “covering, fence”); vat “like”
4.2.50.tr: Jalpa and vitaṇḍā are for guarding the ascertainment of truth, as a fence of thorny branches protects sprouting seeds.
4.2.50.ex: Jalpa and vitaṇḍā are justified by the work they do: like a thorny fence round a seedling, they protect the truth from attack.
